records.old: The red-stained rings in our Kisumu maize stem cross-section (the anchoring phenomenon) are XYLEM — they carry only water and mineral salts upward. The colourless outer tissue of the vascular bundle is PHLOEM — it carries sugars made by photosynthesis to the rest of the plant by translocation. Together, these two systems explain how the maize plant sustains every living cell: xylem supplies water and minerals for photosynthesis; phloem distributes the glucose produced. The polythene-bag water droplets (transpiration, second part of the phenomenon) will be fully explained in Lesson 5

records.why: The lesson said root pressure is why the red dye rose, and later said root pressure is too weak for a 2 m plant. Both are wrong. Root pressure is only about 0.05-0.2 MPa, is strongest at night and is weak or absent by day, when the xylem sap is under tension (pulled) in a transpiring plant, so it cannot be the main force that raised the dye. And holding a 2 m column of water needs only about 0.02 MPa (1000 x 9.8 x 2 = 19.6 kPa = 0.0196 MPa), ten times less than the 0.2 MPa the old reflection note stated. Checked twice: recomputed the pressure and compared with the textbook range for root pressure. The fix keeps the planned teaching order (root pressure first, transpiration pull in Lesson 7) but states the idea correctly everywhere it appears.

records.old: Then ask: 'Why would a maize farmer in Eldoret who never adds DAP see slower water transport than one who does?' Cold-call ONE learner. records.new: Then ask: 'A farmer in Eldoret applies DAP at planting. Phosphate is much more concentrated inside the root hair cell than in the soil water. Which process moves it in, and what must the cell supply?' Cold-call ONE learner. Accept answers, then clarify: phosphate ions enter via active transport, which needs energy (ATP from respiration) because the ions move against the concentration gradient. records.old: kills the plant above the cut by blocking phloem translocation while leaving xylem intact.
records.new: eventually kills the whole plant: blocking the phloem stops sugar reaching the roots below the cut, so the roots starve and die, while the xylem above the cut keeps carrying water to the leaves for a time.
records.why: The old sentence said girdling kills the plant 'above the cut'. The tissue above the cut keeps getting water (xylem is intact) and sugar from its own leaves; it is the roots below the cut that are cut off from sugar, starve, and then the whole plant dies. This also matches the Final Explanation exemplar and the answer now given in Lesson 4.
records.reference: Taiz & Zeiger, Plant Physiology and Development, phloem transport (effects of girdling); KICD Grade 10 curriculum design, Biology 2.2 (girdling to demonstrate translocation)

value.criterion: Scientific accuracy of the transport explanation
value.excellent: Exceeds expectations: correctly explains osmosis, active transport, root pressure (a gentle push, not the main force by day), transpiration pull, and the roles of xylem and phloem, with all key terms used accurately and the links between them made clear.
value.proficient: Meets expectations: explains most processes correctly, with minor errors or one missing mechanism.
value.developing: Approaches expectations: explanation has major errors, or confuses xylem and phloem, or osmosis and active transport.

value.criterion: Use of evidence from the lessons
value.excellent: Exceeds expectations: consistently links claims to the red-dye maize stem, the polythene bag, the girdling demonstration and the transpiration group results (test and control stems).
value.proficient: Meets expectations: refers to some of the evidence, but links are sometimes unclear.
value.developing: Approaches expectations: little or no reference to class evidence.

value.excellent: Exceeds expectations: explains the effect of wind, humidity, light and blocked stomata using the water vapour concentration gradient, and gives three uses of transpiration.
value.proficient: Meets expectations: describes the effect of the factors, with a partial explanation of the gradient or fewer uses.
value.developing: Approaches expectations: only lists results without a mechanism.

value.criterion: Linking to the driving question and Kenyan context
value.excellent: Exceeds expectations: gives a coherent whole-journey explanation, a clear labelled diagram, and sensible advice that respects what Kenyan farmers already know.
value.proficient: Meets expectations: gives a mostly complete journey with a diagram and some context.
value.developing: Approaches expectations: explanation is fragmented, with a missing or unclear diagram and no application.

value.excellent: Exceeds expectations: writes clearly in logical order with correct scientific vocabulary.
value.proficient: Meets expectations: writing is mostly clear with some vocabulary slips.
value.developing: Approaches expectations: writing is hard to follow and vocabulary is mostly everyday.
